KP19 The Nonlinear SVM and the Mercer Kernel Trick

Level: undergraduate, year 3

Pattern Recognition | Chapter 4, §4.18

Slides: read and download

Learning objectives

  • Explain that the SVM rule uses only inner products and state the inner-product identity of the quadratic map.
  • State Mercer's theorem and what it does not tell us, and write the dual problem and the rule of the kernelized SVM.
  • Use experimental numbers to explain the choice of kernel, the effect of the hyperparameters γ\gammaγ and CCC, and the cost and the limit of the kernel trick.

KP19 The Nonlinear SVM and the Mercer Kernel Trick

One-sentence summary: The SVM computes with inner products only, so replace the inner product by a kernel function; we then design a linear classifier in a high-dimensional space that we never visit, and the cost does not depend on the dimension of that space.

1. Inner products only

Plain explanation: Is there a way to keep only a few points and still classify nonlinearly?

  • Support vectors: the training points whose weight λi>0\lambda_i>0λi​>0 after training; the rule depends on them alone, and there are usually far fewer than all the training points.

The rule is g(x)=∑i=1Nsλiyi xiTx+w0g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\lambda_iy_i\,x_i^Tx+w_0g(x)=∑i=1Ns​​λi​yi​xiT​x+w0​ with xxx of dimension lll and NsN_sNs​ support vectors; the data enter only through the inner product xiTxx_i^TxxiT​x. To design in a kkk-dimensional mapped space, replace the vectors by their images yyy and the inner product by yiTyy_i^TyyiT​y. The naive worry: k≫lk\gg lk≫l, so surely the cost explodes?

Figure lec05-kp19-inner: the flow of the rule, with the data entering only through inner products.

2. A quadratic map

Kernel function K(x,z)K(x,z)K(x,z): a function that gives the mapped inner product ϕ(x)Tϕ(z)\phi(x)^T\phi(z)ϕ(x)Tϕ(z) directly, without computing the map first. Example: for y=[x12,2x1x2,x22]Ty=[x_1^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2,x_2^2]^Ty=[x12​,2​x1​x2​,x22​]T, yiTyj=(xiTxj)2y_i^Ty_j=(x_i^Tx_j)^2yiT​yj​=(xiT​xj​)2. Check: xi=(1,2)x_i=(1,2)xi​=(1,2), xj=(2,1)x_j=(2,1)xj​=(2,1): yi=(1,2.828,4)y_i=(1,2.828,4)yi​=(1,2.828,4), yj=(4,2.828,1)y_j=(4,2.828,1)yj​=(4,2.828,1), inner product 4+8+4=164+8+4=164+8+4=16; in the original space (xiTxj)2=42=16(x_i^Tx_j)^2=4^2=16(xiT​xj​)2=42=16, the same. The high-dimensional inner product comes from the original-space inner product, so the entry fee is zero.

3. Lifting the rings

Example (designed here): two concentric rings of radius about 1 and 2 (sd 0.25), 60 training and a separate 100 new points per class. After the map y1+y3=x12+x22=∥x∥2y_1+y_3=x_1^2+x_2^2=\|x\|^2y1​+y3​=x12​+x22​=∥x∥2, so the map turns the radius into a coordinate; the line y1+y3=2.5y_1+y_3=2.5y1​+y3​=2.5 cuts between the rings. One cut gets 97.5% of 200 new points (100 per class) right, a few overlapping at the edges; a plane in 3-D is a circle in the original space. The figure leaves out the middle coordinate 2x1x2\sqrt2x_1x_22​x1​x2​.

Figure lec05-kp19-lift: the rings on the left, and on the right the coordinates y1y_1y1​ and y3y_3y3​ after the map.

4. Mercer's theorem

Mercer condition: KKK is symmetric and continuous and ∬K(x,z)g(x)g(z) dx dz≥0\iint K(x,z)g(x)g(z)\,dx\,dz\ge0∬K(x,z)g(x)g(z)dxdz≥0 for every square-integrable ggg. Formal definition (theorem): a KKK meeting the condition has a space HHH (called an RKHS) and a map ϕ\phiϕ with K(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩K(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangleK(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩, and conversely. What the theorem does not say: what ϕ\phiϕ looks like or the dimension of HHH; the Gaussian kernel's HHH is infinite-dimensional. A finite check (added): the Gram matrix [K(xi,xj)][K(x_i,x_j)][K(xi​,xj​)] must be positive semidefinite; for 30 random points the smallest eigenvalue is 8.8×10−88.8\times10^{-8}8.8×10−8 for the Gaussian kernel and −8×10−15-8\times10^{-15}−8×10−15 for the quadratic one (rounding, taken as 0).

Figure lec05-kp19-mercer: the content of the theorem, what it leaves unsaid and the smallest Gram eigenvalue of two kernels.

5. The kernelized SVM

Common kernels: polynomial (xTz+1)q(x^Tz+1)^q(xTz+1)q; Gaussian exp⁡(−γ∥x−z∥2)\exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)exp(−γ∥x−z∥2); hyperbolic tangent tanh⁡(βxTz+γ)\tanh(\beta x^Tz+\gamma)tanh(βxTz+γ) (may be illegal, see the extension). The dual problem:

max⁡λ ∑iλi−12∑i,jλiλjyiyjK(xi,xj),0≤λi≤C, ∑iλiyi=0, \max_\lambda\ \sum_i\lambda_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_jy_iy_jK(x_i,x_j),\quad 0\le\lambda_i\le C,\ \sum_i\lambda_iy_i=0, λmax​ i∑​λi​−21​i,j∑​λi​λj​yi​yj​K(xi​,xj​),0≤λi​≤C, i∑​λi​yi​=0,

where CCC caps the penalty for violations. The rule is g(x)=∑i=1NsλiyiK(xi,x)+w0g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\lambda_iy_iK(x_i,x)+w_0g(x)=∑i=1Ns​​λi​yi​K(xi​,x)+w0​, and g>0g>0g>0 goes to ω1\omega_1ω1​. Check (added): with the solved λ\lambdaλ this formula differs from the library's decision value by at most 10−1410^{-14}10−14. Because the kernel is nonlinear, this is a nonlinear classifier in the original space.

6. The rings experiment

Example (designed here): concentric rings, 60 training and 500 new points per class; C=10C=10C=10, Gaussian γ=0.5\gamma=0.5γ=0.5, quadratic kernel (xTz+1)2(x^Tz+1)^2(xTz+1)2. Accuracy on new points: the linear kernel 56.2% with 118 support vectors; the quadratic 97.6% with 10; the Gaussian 96.8% with 19. Same data and algorithm, only the kernel changes, from near guessing to about 97%; the Gaussian kernel keeps 19 support vectors where a PNN keeps all 120 training points (compare KP21).

Figure lec05-kp19-regions: the decision regions and support vectors (circles) of three kernels.

7. Hyperparameters

Hyperparameter: a parameter set before training rather than solved from the data, here the Gaussian γ\gammaγ and the penalty cap CCC. Example (designed here): rings that overlap more (sd 0.45), C=10C=10C=10, sweeping γ\gammaγ. Accuracy on training and new points: γ=0.1\gamma=0.1γ=0.1: 88.3%, 87.0% (best); γ=10\gamma=10γ=10: 98.3%, 79.4%; γ=50\gamma=50γ=50: 99.2%, 74.7%. Sweeping CCC at γ=0.5\gamma=0.5γ=0.5, new points: C=0.01C=0.01C=0.01: 84.3%; C=1C=1C=1: 86.4% (best); C=1000C=1000C=1000: 82.8%. The best values were picked on the new points; in practice use separate validation data. Common misconception: the higher the training accuracy the better; when γ\gammaγ is too large the training fit tightens and the new points get worse.

Figure lec05-kp19-hyper: training and new-point accuracy against the Gaussian γ\gammaγ.

8. Dimension-free

A polynomial kernel of dimension lll and degree qqq has (l+qq)\binom{l+q}{q}(ql+q​) features: (l,q)=(2,2)(l,q)=(2,2)(l,q)=(2,2): 6; (10,3)(10,3)(10,3): 286; (100,5)(100,5)(100,5): 96,560,646; (784,5)(784,5)(784,5): 2,515,874,132,157 (about 2.5×10122.5\times10^{12}2.5×1012). One kernel value is an inner product and a power, about lll multiplications whatever the kernel-space dimension; the infinite-dimensional Gaussian space still costs one distance. Limit: training still needs an N×NN\times NN×N Gram matrix, and nobody knows how to pick the best kernel. To remember: kernel trick = any algorithm that uses only inner products gets higher dimensions for free; the price is not knowing which space you are in.

Figure lec05-kp19-cost: explicit features of a polynomial kernel against the multiplications of one kernel value.

Extension: an illegal kernel, practice and worked solution

The tanh kernel can be illegal (designed here): K=tanh⁡(2xTz+1)K=\tanh(2x^Tz+1)K=tanh(2xTz+1) on the three points (−1,0)(-1,0)(−1,0), (1.6,0.9)(1.6,0.9)(1.6,0.9), (0.1,−0.8)(0.1,-0.8)(0.1,−0.8) gives a Gram matrix with eigenvalues −0.132-0.132−0.132, 0.8750.8750.875 and 2.2322.2322.232; the negative one violates the Mercer condition. With 10 random points drawn 200 times the tanh kernel has a negative eigenvalue in all 200 draws and the Gaussian kernel in none. The hyperbolic tangent with (β=2,γ=1)(\beta=2,\gamma=1)(β=2,γ=1) is not a legal kernel and the dual problem need not be convex (a theoretical inference, not measured here); check before using it, or use the Gaussian kernel.

Figure lec05-kp19-tanh: the Gram matrix and eigenvalues of three points.

Practice: K(x,z)=(xTz+1)2K(x,z)=(x^Tz+1)^2K(x,z)=(xTz+1)2, x=(1,2)x=(1,2)x=(1,2), z=(3,1)z=(3,1)z=(3,1); the map ϕ(x)=[1,2x1,2x2,x12,2x1x2,x22]\phi(x)=[1,\sqrt2x_1,\sqrt2x_2,x_1^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2,x_2^2]ϕ(x)=[1,2​x1​,2​x2​,x12​,2​x1​x2​,x22​].

  1. Compute K(x,z)K(x,z)K(x,z) directly with the kernel.
  2. Compute the 6 features ϕ(x)\phi(x)ϕ(x) and ϕ(z)\phi(z)ϕ(z), take their inner product and check it against question 1.

Figure lec05-kp19-practice: the setup of the practice.

Worked solution of questions 1 and 2: (1) xTz=1⋅3+2⋅1=5x^Tz=1\cdot3+2\cdot1=5xTz=1⋅3+2⋅1=5 and K=(5+1)2=36K=(5+1)^2=36K=(5+1)2=36, with only 2 multiplications. (2) ϕ(x)=(1,1.414,2.828,1,2.828,4)\phi(x)=(1,1.414,2.828,1,2.828,4)ϕ(x)=(1,1.414,2.828,1,2.828,4) and ϕ(z)=(1,4.243,1.414,9,4.243,1)\phi(z)=(1,4.243,1.414,9,4.243,1)ϕ(z)=(1,4.243,1.414,9,4.243,1); the inner product is 1+6+4+9+12+4=361+6+4+9+12+4=361+6+4+9+12+4=36, the same as question 1. (3) Check: the same 36; the kernel works in 2-D while the map first builds 6 features, and the gap widens with dimension.
